title: When the marketing site and the product disagree
metaTitle: When the site and the product disagree
excerpt: Buyers feel the seam when the homepage is quiet and the product is loud. Carry one idea from the first screen into the buttons, empty states, and errors.
alt: A wide city avenue with yellow taxis, tall buildings, and people on the sidewalk, one street at two speeds for an article about a site and a product that must share an idea.
caption: One avenue, more than one speed of traffic. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What does it mean when the marketing site and the product feel different?
faqs.answer: It means a buyer is meeting two ideas, such as a quiet homepage and a dense app full of internal names. The seam shows up at login, in the first empty screen, and in the words on buttons. People experience it as doubt, even when both pieces are well made on their own.

faqs.question: Should the product look exactly like the marketing site?
faqs.answer: They should share one idea, one type system, and one vocabulary for the same actions. The product can be denser because people stay to work, and the marketing page can have more air. Density and air are not a license to rename the product's buttons.

faqs.question: What should you fix first?
faqs.answer: Write the one sentence the company is willing to repeat, then check the homepage and the main workflow against it. Align the words for the primary action before you commission a new visual system. A new coat on two conflicting sentences makes the conflict more expensive.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A marketing site product mismatch is the seam a buyer feels when the homepage promised one company and the interface delivers another. Sometimes the site is quiet and the product is loud. Sometimes the site is a carnival and the product is a spreadsheet. The person notices at the moment they decided to trust you.

Pick one idea and carry it across. Type, color, and the words on buttons, empty states, and errors should survive the trip from the first screen into the tool.

## Where the seam shows up

The seam is rarely a logo mismatch. Logos are the easy part. The seam is behavioral. The site spoke in short, careful sentences, and the app opens on twelve equal cards with labels only an internal team would use. Or the site shouted a transformation, and the product opens on a blank table with no hint of that promise.

Watch the first minute after signup, not the brand review. [Nielsen Norman Group's research](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) is about web pages, and the lesson holds at this threshold. People often leave within 10 to 20 seconds, and a value proposition has to be clear within about 10 seconds to earn a longer look. A value they understood on the homepage has to be visible again inside about the same breath. If the product opens on a tour of the whole system, the promise they just believed is gone.

You can see the seam in support. Tickets that start with "I thought this would" are design evidence. So are sales calls that apologize for the interface. The apology means the site sold a feeling the product does not keep. Fixing the script leaves the seam in place for the next buyer.

Founders often split the work across two years, or two vendors, and then act surprised. The marketing site was a project. The product was a different project. Nobody owned the sentence that was supposed to survive both. The clashing colors are the symptom. The missing sentence is the cause.

## Choose the idea you will carry

Write one sentence the company can repeat. A behavior, not a slogan contest. This product is calm enough to read. This product is dense because the buyer's job is dense. This product shows only what changed and what needs a decision. The sentence should be specific enough that a quiet manuscript and a loud gradient cannot both satisfy it.

Hanabi's public line, clarity over complexity, is one example you can test. On a marketing page it means the offer is understandable before the decoration. In a product it means the primary action is obvious and the rare path is quiet. Your sentence can be different. It has to be checkable by a teammate who was not in the room.

Test it against a real screen and a real homepage section, side by side. If you have to add that marketing is allowed to be a different company, you do not have one idea yet. You have a truce. Truces show up later as a second visual language nobody budgeted to maintain.

Wabisabi, as a public brand world, is calm and tactile. A product attached to that world would break the idea if the app opened in neon. Got Next and Leadly, as public product interfaces, carry a more instrumental calm. The lesson is not to copy either. The lesson is that the public surface and the working surface can be the same thought.

## Carry type, color, and the words

Pick one type system. A display face on the site and a UI face in the product can work when the text face is shared and the sizes feel related. Two unrelated families feel like two companies sharing a login. Write down the sizes you actually use: a page title, a section title, body, and a label. Four sizes that appear in both places beat a poster scale the app will never touch.

Color should mean the same thing in both places. If a strong color is the action on the site, it should be the action in the product. If the site uses that color as decoration on every illustration, the product has no signal left. Limit the accent. Document the neutrals. A founder should be able to open both and see one palette under two levels of density.

Then the words, which is where seams hide. The same action needs the same name. [The W3C's WCAG overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) describes understandable content in principles a team can use without a certification project: people should be able to perceive the interface, operate it, and understand it. Consistent names are part of understanding. "Start" on the site and "Initialize workspace" in the app is a small betrayal on every new user.

Write a short list of the words you will use for the primary objects. The thing the customer has many of. The action that creates one. The action that invites a colleague. Put that list where marketing and product both edit. Twelve words, pinned, will do more than a glossary nobody opens.

## The moment someone logs in

Design the threshold on purpose. The person has just left a page that made a promise. The first product screen should acknowledge that promise in the product's own materials. One sentence at the top of an empty state, in the same voice as the homepage, plus the single action that fulfills it. A tour of every menu is a second product they did not ask to learn.

Empty, error, and success are where voice either holds or collapses. An error that says something went wrong, after a homepage that was specific, is a costume change. An error that says what happened and what to do next is the same company, under stress. Write those three states before you write more feature pages. They are the screens people remember.

Motion should agree as well. If the site is still and editorial, a product full of bouncing cards feels like a different building. If you use motion, keep it short, show where a panel came from, and respect a request for reduced motion. Decorative loops that ignore that setting are a craft failure on either surface.

Performance belongs in the same idea. A marketing page that loads the offer quickly, and a product that spends its first second on a spinner, tell two stories about respect. You do not need a lab score in the guidelines. You need someone to open the handoff on an ordinary phone and admit what they see.

## A short audit you can run this week

Put the homepage and the main workflow on one table. Screenshot both. Read them aloud. You are listening for a change of speaker.

Check these, in order:

1. The first sentence on the site and the first sentence in the product. Do they describe the same job?
2. The primary button. Same verb, same color role, same outcome.
3. One empty state. Does it offer the next step in the site's voice?
4. One error. Does it name the problem in words a customer can repeat?
5. Type and accent, at arm's length. One family, or two companies?

Fix the words first. Renaming a button and rewriting an empty state can close more of the seam than a rebrand. If the type and color fail badly, you have a system problem, and that is a project. Do not start it until the sentence is agreed, or you will restyle the conflict.

Invite one person who only knows the marketing site to complete the core task in the product. Do not help. Where they hesitate is the seam, even if your critique would have pointed somewhere more sophisticated. Write down their words. Those words are better button copy than a workshop that never opened the app.

## Differences that are allowed

The product can be denser. People come to it to work, and they learn the layout. The marketing site can have more air, because it is introducing a stranger. Density and air can share a type ramp and a palette. What should not differ is the personality of the decisions: what you emphasize, what you refuse, how you talk when something fails.

Photography can live mostly on the site. Illustration can be scarcer in the product, where it competes with data. That is a fair difference. An illustration style that contradicts the product's tone is not. If the site is full of soft characters and the product is a serious ledger, choose which company you are and let the other surface follow.

Navigation will differ because the jobs differ. The site routes toward a conversation or a signup. The product routes toward the work. The same function, when it appears in both, should keep its name and a familiar place. A help link, an account menu, a way back to the work. Inventing new chrome for the app because it felt like a fresh start is how the seam gets a frame.

You can ship one surface first and let the other catch up, as long as the lag is named. A note that the visual system is mid-change is honest for a month. A year of two systems is a decision to confuse people. Put a date on the catch-up, and give one person the job of saying when a screen has crossed over.

## Fix the sentence, then the skin

Start with the sentence. Then the shared words. Then the type and color on the screens people actually see: homepage, signup, the main workflow, empty, error. A full rebrand in the middle of this is often a way to avoid the sentence. You can tell, because the workshops produce adjectives and the empty state still says there is nothing here.

On a Hanabi project, brand and interface are one engagement when the founder wants them to be one idea. Structure is cheap to change in Figma. Type, real content, and motion tell the truth in the browser. A marketing site in Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind can share tokens with the product instead of inventing a second palette in a tool you will regret.

The seam often shows up again in the form that asks for a demo, because that form is the door between the two worlds. How to design that door is the next piece, [designing a demo request that respects time](/blog/designing-a-demo-request-that-respects-time). Read it if the homepage is calm and the form is a questionnaire from a different company.

When you want help carrying one idea from the public page into the interface, look at [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). The test is simple. Would a buyer recognize the product as the thing the site just described, without you in the room to translate.
